{{short description|Cryptographic hash function}}
{{Other uses|LSH (disambiguation)}}
'''LSH''' is a [[cryptographic hash function]] designed in 2014 by [[South Korea]] to provide integrity in general-purpose software environments such as [[Personal computer|PCs]] and [[smart device]]s.<ref name="KHL+14">{{cite book |last1=Kim |first1=Dong-Chan |last2=Hong |first2=Deukjo |last3=Lee |first3=Jung-Keun |last4=Kim |first4=Woo-Hwan |last5=Kwon |first5=Daesung |title=Information Security and Cryptology - ICISC 2014 |chapter=LSH: A New Fast Secure Hash Function Family |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2015 |volume=8949 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-319-15943-0 |pages=286–313 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-15943-0_18 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-15943-0_18 |language=en}}</ref> LSH is one of the cryptographic algorithms approved by the Korean Cryptographic Module Validation Program (KCMVP).
And it is the national standard of South Korea (KS X 3262).

== Specification ==

The overall structure of the hash function LSH is shown in the following figure.

[[File:LSH_structure.png|600px|thumb|center|Overall structure of LSH]]

The hash function LSH has the wide-pipe Merkle-Damgård structure with one-zeros padding.
The message hashing process of LSH consists of the following three stages.

# ''Initialization'':
#* One-zeros padding of a given bit string message.
#* Conversion to 32-word array message blocks from the padded bit string message.
#* Initialization of a chaining variable with the initialization vector.
# ''Compression'':
#* Updating of chaining variables by iteration of a compression function with message blocks.
# ''Finalization'':
#* Generation of an <math> n </math>-bit hash value from the final chaining variable.

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: left; margin-left: auto; margin-right:auto; border: none;"
|
* '''function''' Hash function LSH
* '''input:''' Bit string message <math> m </math>
* '''output:''' Hash value <math> h \in \{ 0, 1 \}^n </math>
* '''procedure'''
<math> \qquad </math>One-zeros padding of <math> m </math>

<math> \qquad </math>Generation of <math> t </math> message blocks <math> \{ \textsf{M}^{(i)} \}_{i=0}^{t-1} </math>, where <math> t = \Big\lceil \frac{|m| + 1}{32w} \Big\rceil </math> from the padded bit string

<math> \qquad </math><math> \textsf{CV}^{(0)} \leftarrow \textsf{IV} </math>

<math> \qquad </math>'''for''' <math> i = 0 </math> '''to''' <math> (t-1) </math> '''do'''

<math> \qquad </math><math> \qquad </math><math> \textsf{CV}^{(i+1)} \leftarrow \textrm{CF} (\textsf{CV}^{(i)}, \textsf{M}^{(i)}) </math>

<math> \qquad </math>'''end for'''

<math> \qquad </math><math> h \leftarrow \textrm{FIN}_n(\textsf{CV}^{(t)}) </math>

<math> \qquad </math>'''return''' <math> h </math>
|}

===Initialization===

Let <math> m </math> be a given bit string message.
The given <math> m </math> is padded by one-zeros, i.e., the bit ‘1’ is appended to the end of <math> m </math>, and the bit ‘0’s are appended until a bit length of a padded message is <math> 32wt </math>, where <math> t = \lceil (|m| + 1)/32w\rceil </math> and <math> \lceil x \rceil </math> is the smallest integer not less than <math> x </math>.

Let <math> m_p = m_0 \| m_1 \| \ldots \| m_{(32wt-1)} </math> be the one-zeros-padded <math> 32wt </math>-bit string of <math> m </math>.
Then <math> m_p </math> is considered as a <math> 4wt </math>-byte array <math> m_a = (m[0], \ldots , m[4wt-1]) </math>, where <math> m[k] = m_{8k} \| m_{(8k+1)} \| \ldots \| m_{(8k+7)} </math> for all <math> 0 \le k \le (4wt-1) </math>.
The <math> 4wt </math>-byte array <math>m_a</math> converts into a <math> 32t </math>-word array <math> \textsf{M} = (M[0], \ldots , M[32t-1]) </math> as follows.

<math>M[s] \leftarrow m[ws/8+(w/8-1)] \| \ldots \| m[ws/8+1] \| m[ws/8]</math> <math>(0 \le s \le (32t-1))</math>

From the word array <math> \textsf{M} </math>, we define the <math> t </math> 32-word array message blocks <math> \{ \textsf{M}^{(i)} \}_{i=0}^{t-1} </math> as follows.

<math> \textsf{M}^{(i)} \leftarrow (M[32i], M[32i+1], \ldots , M[32i+31])</math> <math>(0 \le i \le (t-1))</math>

The 16-word array chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(0)} </math> is initialized to the initialization vector <math> \textsf{IV} </math>.

<math> \textsf{CV}^{(0)}[l] \leftarrow \textsf{IV}[l]</math> <math>(0 \le l \le 15)</math>

The initialization vector <math> \textsf{IV} </math> is as follows.
In the following tables, all values are expressed in hexadecimal form.

===Compression===

In this stage, the <math> t </math> 32-word array message blocks <math> \{ \textsf{M}^{(i)} \}_{i=0}^{t-1} </math>, which are generated from a message <math> m </math> in the initialization stage, are compressed by iteration of compression functions.
The compression function <math> \textrm{CF} : \mathcal{W}^{16} \times \mathcal{W}^{32} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16}</math> has two inputs; the <math> i </math>-th 16-word chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(i)} </math> and the <math> i </math>-th 32-word message block <math> \textsf{M}^{(i)} </math>.
And it returns the <math> (i+1) </math>-th 16-word chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(i+1)} </math>.
Here and subsequently, <math> \mathcal{W}^t </math> denotes the set of all <math> t </math>-word arrays for <math> t \ge 1 </math>.

The following four functions are used in a compression function:

* Message expansion function <math>\textrm{MsgExp}: \mathcal{W}^{32} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16(Ns+1)}</math>
* Message addition function <math>\textrm{MsgAdd}: \mathcal{W}^{16} \times \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16}</math>
* Mix function <math>\textrm{Mix}_j: \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16}</math>
* Word-permutation function <math>\textrm{WordPerm}: \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16}</math>

The overall structure of the compression function is shown in the following figure.

[[File:LSH structure of the compression function.png|600px|thumb|center|Compression function of LSH]]

In a compression function, the message expansion function <math> \textrm{MsgExp} </math> generates <math> (N_s+1) </math> 16-word array sub-messages <math> \{ \textsf{M}_j^{(i)} \}_{j=0}^{N_s} </math> from given <math> \textsf{M}^{(i)} </math>.
Let <math> \textsf{T} = (T[0], \ldots , T[15]) </math> be a temporary 16-word array set to the <math> i </math>-th chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(i)} </math>.
The <math> j </math>-th step function <math> \textrm{Step}_j </math> having two inputs <math> \textsf{T} </math> and <math> \textsf{M}_j^{(i)} </math> updates <math> \textsf{T} </math>, i.e., <math> \textsf{T} \leftarrow \textrm{Step}_j \left( \textsf{T}, \textsf{M}_j^{(i)} \right) </math>.
All step functions are proceeded in order <math> j = 0, \ldots, N_s - 1 </math>.
Then one more <math> \textrm{MsgAdd} </math> operation by <math> \textsf{M}_{N_s}^{(i)} </math> is proceeded, and the <math> (i+1) </math>-th chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(i+1)} </math> is set to <math> \textsf{T} </math>.
The process of a compression function in detail is as follows.

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: left; margin-left: auto; margin-right:auto; border: none;"
|
* '''function''' Compression function <math> \textrm{CF} </math>
* '''input:''' The <math> i </math>-th chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(i)} \in \mathcal{W}^{16} </math> and the <math> i </math>-th message block <math> \textsf{M}^{(i)} \in \mathcal{W}^{32} </math>
* '''output:''' The <math> (i + 1) </math>-th chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(i+1)} \in \mathcal{W}^{16} </math>
* '''procedure'''
<math> \qquad </math><math> \{ \textsf{M}_j^{(i)} \}_{j=0}^{N_s} \leftarrow \textrm{MsgExp} \left( \textsf{M}^{(i)} \right) </math>

<math> \qquad </math><math> \textsf{T} \leftarrow \textsf{CV}^{(i)} </math>

<math> \qquad </math>'''for''' <math> j = 0 </math> '''to''' <math> (N_s - 1) </math> '''do'''

<math> \qquad </math><math> \qquad </math><math> \textsf{T} \leftarrow \textrm{Step}_j \left( \textsf{T}, \textsf{M}_j^{(i)} \right) </math>

<math> \qquad </math>'''end for'''

<math> \qquad </math><math> \textsf{CV}^{(i+1)} \leftarrow \textrm{MsgAdd} \left( \textsf{T}, \textsf{M}_{N_s}^{(i)} \right) </math>

<math> \qquad </math>'''return''' <math> \textsf{CV}^{(i+1)} </math>
|}

Here the <math> j </math>-th step function <math> \textrm{Step}_j : \mathcal{W}^{16} \times \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16} </math> is as follows.

<math> \textrm{Step}_j := \textrm{WordPerm} \circ \textrm{Mix}_j \circ \textrm{MsgAdd}</math> <math>(0 \le j \le (N_s-1)) </math>

The following figure shows the <math> j </math>-th step function <math> \textrm{Step}_j </math> of a compression function.

[[File:LSH step function.png|600px|thumb|center|The <math> j </math>-th step function <math> \textrm{Step}_j </math>]]

====Message Expansion Function MsgExp====

Let <math> \textsf{M}^{(i)} = ( M^{(i)}[0], \ldots , M^{(i)}[31] ) </math> be the <math> i </math>-th 32-word array message block.
The message expansion function <math> \textrm{MsgExp} </math> generates <math> (N_s + 1) </math> 16-word array sub-messages <math> \{ \textsf{M}_j^{(i)} \}_{j=0}^{N_s} </math> from a message block <math> \textsf{M}^{(i)} </math>.
The first two sub-messages <math> \textsf{M}_{0}^{(i)} = ( M_{0}^{(i)}[0], \ldots , M_{0}^{(i)}[15] ) </math> and <math> \textsf{M}_{1}^{(i)} = ( M_{1}^{(i)}[0], \ldots , M_{1}^{(i)}[15] ) </math> are defined as follows.

* <math> \textsf{M}_0^{(i)} \leftarrow (M^{(i)}[0], M^{(i)}[1], \ldots , M^{(i)}[15])</math>
* <math> \textsf{M}_1^{(i)} \leftarrow (M^{(i)}[16], M^{(i)}[17], \ldots , M^{(i)}[31])</math>

The next sub-messages <math> \{ \textsf{M}_j^{(i)} = ( M_{j}^{(i)}[0], \ldots , M_{j}^{(i)}[15] ) \}_{j=2}^{N_s} </math> are generated as follows.

* <math> \textsf{M}_j^{(i)}[l] \leftarrow \textsf{M}_{j-1}^{(i)}[l] \boxplus\textsf{M}_{j-2}^{(i)}[\tau(l)]</math> <math>(0 \le l \le 15, \ 2 \le j \le N_s)</math>

Here <math> \tau </math> is the permutation over <math> \mathbb{Z}_{16} </math> defined as follows.

====Message Addition Function MsgAdd====

For two 16-word arrays <math> \textsf{X} = (X[0], \ldots , X[15]) </math> and <math> \textsf{Y} = (Y[0], \ldots , Y[15]) </math>, the message addition function <math> \textrm{MsgAdd} : \mathcal{W}^{16} \times \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16} </math> is defined as follows.

<math> \textrm{MsgAdd}( \textsf{X}, \textsf{Y} ) := (X[0] \oplus Y[0], \ldots , X[15] \oplus Y[15]) </math>

====Mix Function Mix====

The <math> j </math>-th mix function <math> \textrm{Mix}_j: \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16} </math> updates the 16-word array <math> \textsf{T} = (T[0], \ldots , T[15]) </math> by mixing every two-word pair; <math> T[l] </math> and <math> T[l+8] </math> for <math> (0 \le l < 8) </math>.
For <math> 0 \le j < N_s </math>, the mix function <math> \textrm{Mix}_j </math> proceeds as follows.

<math> (T[l], T[l+8]) \leftarrow \textrm{Mix}_{j,l}(T[l], T[l+8]) </math> <math>(0 \le l < 8) </math>

Here <math> \textrm{Mix}_{j,l} </math> is a two-word mix function.
Let <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math> be words.
The two-word mix function <math> \textrm{Mix}_{j,l} : \mathcal{W}^2 \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^2 </math> is defined as follows.

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: left; margin-left: auto; margin-right:auto; border: none;"
|
* '''function''' Two-word mix function <math> \textrm{Mix}_{j,l} </math>
* '''input:'''  Words <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math>
* '''output:''' Words <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math>
* '''procedure'''
<math> \qquad </math><math> X \leftarrow X \boxplus Y </math>;<math> \qquad X \leftarrow X^{\lll \alpha_j} </math>;

<math> \qquad </math><math> X \leftarrow X \oplus SC_j[l] </math>;

<math> \qquad </math><math> Y \leftarrow X \boxplus Y </math>;<math> \qquad Y \leftarrow Y^{\lll \beta_j} </math>;

<math> \qquad </math><math> X \leftarrow X \boxplus Y </math>;<math> \qquad Y \leftarrow Y^{\lll \gamma_l} </math>;

<math> \qquad </math>'''return''' <math> X </math>, <math> Y </math>;
|}

====Word-Permutation Function WordPerm====

Let <math> \textsf{X} = (X[0], \ldots , X[15]) </math> be a 16-word array.
The word-permutation function <math> \textrm{WordPerm} : \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \mathcal{W}^{16} </math> is defined as follows.

<math> \textrm{WordPerm}( \textsf{X}) = (X[\sigma(0)], \ldots , X[\sigma(15)]) </math>

===Finalization===

The finalization function <math> \textrm{FIN}_n : \mathcal{W}^{16} \rightarrow \{0, 1\}^{n} </math> returns <math> n </math>-bit hash value <math> h </math> from the final chaining variable <math> \textsf{CV}^{(t)} = ( CV^{(t)}[0], \ldots , CV^{(t)}[15])</math>.
When <math> \textsf{H} = (H[0], \ldots , H[7]) </math> is an 8-word variable and <math> \textsf{h}_\textsf{b} = (h_b[0], \ldots , h_b[w-1]) </math> is a <math> w </math>-byte variable, the finalization function <math> \textrm{FIN}_n </math> performs the following procedure.

* <math>H[l] \leftarrow CV^{(t)}[l] \oplus CV^{(t)}[l+8]</math> <math>(0 \le l \le 7)</math>
* <math>h_b[s] \leftarrow H[\lfloor 8s/w\rfloor ]^{\ggg (8s \mod w)}_{[7:0]}</math> <math>(0 \le s \le (w-1))</math>
* <math>h \leftarrow (h_b[0] \| \ldots \| h_b[w-1])_{[0:n-1]}</math>

Here, <math> X_{[i:j]} </math> denotes <math> x_i \| x_{i-1} \| \ldots \| x_j </math>, the sub-bit string of a word <math> X </math> for <math> i \ge j </math>.
And <math> x_{[i:j]} </math> denotes <math> x _i \| x_{i+1} \| \ldots \| x_j </math>, the sub-bit string of a <math> l </math>-bit string <math> x = x_0 \| x_1 \| \ldots \| x_{l-1} </math> for <math> i \le j </math>.

== Security ==

LSH is secure against known attacks on hash functions up to now.
LSH is collision-resistant for <math> q < 2^{n/2} </math> and preimage-resistant and second-preimage-resistant for <math> q < 2^n </math> in the ideal cipher model, where <math> q </math> is a number of queries for LSH structure.<ref name=KHL+14 />
LSH-256 is secure against all the existing hash function attacks when the number of steps is 13 or more, while LSH-512 is secure if the number of steps is 14 or more.
Note that the steps which work as security margin are 50% of the compression function.<ref name=KHL+14 />

== Test vectors ==

Test vectors for LSH for each digest length are as follows.
All values are expressed in hexadecimal form.

LSH-256-224("abc") = <span style="font-family:Courier;">F7 C5 3B A4 03 4E 70 8E 74 FB A4 2E 55 99 7C A5 12 6B B7 62 36 88 F8 53 42 F7 37 32</span>

LSH-256-256("abc") = <span style="font-family:Courier;">5F BF 36 5D AE A5 44 6A 70 53 C5 2B 57 40 4D 77 A0 7A 5F 48 A1 F7 C1 96 3A 08 98 BA 1B 71 47 41</span>

LSH-512-224("abc") = <span style="font-family:Courier;">D1 68 32 34 51 3E C5 69 83 94 57 1E AD 12 8A 8C D5 37 3E 97 66 1B A2 0D CF 89 E4 89</span>

LSH-512-256("abc") = <span style="font-family:Courier;">CD 89 23 10 53 26 02 33 2B 61 3F 1E C1 1A 69 62 FC A6 1E A0 9E CF FC D4 BC F7 58 58 D8 02 ED EC</span>

LSH-512-384("abc") = <span style="font-family:Courier;">5F 34 4E FA A0 E4 3C CD 2E 5E 19 4D 60 39 79 4B 4F B4 31 F1 0F B4 B6 5F D4 5E 9D A4 EC DE 0F 27 B6 6E 8D BD FA 47 25 2E 0D 0B 74 1B FD 91 F9 FE</span>

LSH-512-512("abc") = <span style="font-family:Courier;">A3 D9 3C FE 60 DC 1A AC DD 3B D4 BE F0 A6 98 53 81 A3 96 C7 D4 9D 9F D1 77 79 56 97 C3 53 52 08 B5 C5 72 24 BE F2 10 84 D4 20 83 E9 5A 4B D8 EB 33 E8 69 81 2B 65 03 1C 42 88 19 A1 E7 CE 59 6D</span>

== Implementations ==

LSH is free for any use public or private, commercial or non-commercial.
The source code for distribution of LSH implemented in C, Java, and Python can be downloaded from KISA's cryptography use activation webpage.<ref name="LSH_source">{{Cite web|url=https://seed.kisa.or.kr/kisa/Board/22/detailView.do|title=KISA 암호이용활성화 - 암호알고리즘 소스코드|website=seed.kisa.or.kr}}</ref>

== KCMVP ==

LSH is one of the cryptographic algorithms approved by the Korean Cryptographic Module Validation Program (KCMVP).<ref name="KCMVP">{{Cite web|url=https://seed.kisa.or.kr/kisa/kcmvp/EgovSummary.do|title=KISA 암호이용활성화 - 개요|website=seed.kisa.or.kr}}</ref>

== Standardization ==

LSH is included in the following standard.

* KS X 3262, Hash function LSH (in Korean)<ref name="KS_X_3262">{{cite web
